newsitem.title: USA: IMF warns of risks to European economic growth.
newsitem.headline: IMF warns of risks to European economic growth.

text.p: The IMF said Wednesday it saw signs that European economic growth was starting to pick up but warned that the upswing could be hampered by the drive to meet tough budget goals set out in the Maastricht Treaty.
In its semi-annual World Economic Outlook, the International Monetary Fund forecast that growth throughout the European Union would increase to 2.5 percent next year from 1.6 percent in 1996.

But, it added, "The recovery in Europe may be weaker than projected because it may be restrained ... by the short-term contractionary effects of fiscal consolidation efforts being implemented in most EU countries partly to satisfy the Maastricht criteria by 1997."
Uncertainties about "policy implementation" and concerns about high unemployment may also hamper the recovery, it added.

Under the Maastricht Treaty, governments that wish to be founding members of European Monetary Union in 1999 must reduce their 1997 budget deficits to the equivalent of three percent of gross domestic product, although there is some flexibility built into that target.
The IMF said it expects both Germany and France to meet the three percent target, although it made clear that depended on economic growth picking up as expected.
"The three percent deficit goal (for France) seems within reach provided activity strengthens during the period ahead," it said.
Flemming Larsen, Deputy Director at the IMF's Research Department, was also encouraged by the progress that Italy has made in reining its its bloated budget.
"We are quite optimistic about Italy's medium-term outlook and scope for eventually meeting the (Maastricht) convergence criteria," Larsen told reporters.
But he added that it was difficult to predict precisely when that would occur, because of lack of full information on Italy's budget.
The IMF was gloomy about the outlook for European unemployment, forecasting only a small fall next year and warning that joblessness could even rise if labor markets are not comprehensively reformed.
It expects average unemployment in the European Union of 11 percent next year, compared with 11.4 percent this year.

"The real risk in Europe is that in the absence of comprehensive labor market reforms, unemployment rates could continue their steady upward march," the IMF said. "This underscores the urgency of tackling the problem more forcefully."
It accused European governments of "excessive timidity" in labor market policies and recommended a whole set of possible reforms.

They included: reduced unemployment benefits with tighter eligibility criteria and of shorter duration; lower payroll taxes, particularly for low-wage workers; minimum wage cuts; and changes in the way governments handle collective bargaining agreements.
